title: Chapter 5. Those Who Do Not Want a Chip

blocks.text: The fifth people was born on a cold high plateau, with a dry wind that wasn't the levante and a clear light, almost like March. This time the clone put neither the sea nor the coffee in their chips. He gave them less. He wanted to see what they would do with less inheritance, after the portrait, after the altar, after the dry lagoon. He left them the cultivated body, the language, a trade of stone and garden, and one question, engraved not as dogma but as an ember: *what is a flaw?*

blocks.text: Andrés received the letter while Lía, with his permission, was holding his hand, not to amend the harbour but to keep him company. What arrived was not first a landscape but an argument, already under way, in a square of pale stone.

blocks.text: Part of that people wanted to remove their chips.
blocks.html: Part of that people wanted to remove their chips.

blocks.text: They said it without theatrics, the way you say you want to open a window. The chip, they claimed, was the workshop's mark, Nexum's fingernail, the proof that they were a product and not a people. They wanted to be only body, like the Andrés of the shore (or like they believed the Andrés of the shore to be), a body that feels and makes mistakes without an archive behind the nape of its neck. Another part opposed it: without the chip, they said, the inherited language would go out, and the question, and the little memory of an Earth they had never set foot on. What would be left were beautiful, mute bodies, or bodies with an infancy starting from zero, and that wasn't freedom: it was an erasure.

blocks.text: A woman with a still-fresh scar planted herself in front of the clone.
blocks.html: A woman with a still-fresh scar planted herself in front of the clone.

blocks.text: “You're an artificial brain in a cloned body,” she said, and the exactness hurt Andrés, in his kitchen, like a truth spoken without consent. “She, the one on the shore, is a chip in a cultivated body. We're that too. How long are we going to call ‘children of the Earth’ what the Earth would manufacture on a ship? We want the risk of having no archive. We want to forget for real, not the way you forget when there's still a backup.”

blocks.text: The clone forbade them nothing. He couldn't, having promised not to be an owner. Nor did he encourage them, because encouraging someone to switch themselves off was another way of ruling.
blocks.html: The clone forbade them nothing. He couldn't, having promised not to be an owner. Nor did he encourage them, because encouraging someone to switch themselves off was another way of ruling.

blocks.text: “The chip isn't your soul, if there is a soul,” he said. “It's a tool I left you, and tools can be put down. I'll also tell you the fact, not the opinion: without it, I don't know what will be left of the language, or the question, or yourselves. If you switch it off, let it be one at a time, and let someone stay close, in case the body doesn't know how to be alone.”

blocks.text: Andrés, pale, told Aya with a surgeon's caution. For an instant Aya raised her hand to the nape of her neck, where the scar was so fine you could only see it if you knew where to look.

blocks.text: “They want not to be like me,” she said, without offence, or with an offence so old it no longer burned. “I couldn't switch my chip off. It wasn't a window. It was me. If they can, and they choose not to be me, I won't call them traitors. I'll call them, if anything, brave, or reckless. That isn't for me to decide.”

blocks.text: Lía asked, as the grandmothers had taught her:
blocks.html: Lía asked, as the grandmothers had taught her:

blocks.text: “If they switch off, are they still children of the Earth, or do they become children of that wind? And if they don't, are they more faithful, or just more dependent? Father, he mustn't settle this with a rulebook. It's the same question as my hand: who decides what a flaw is. For some, the chip is the flaw. For others, removing it is.”

blocks.text: On the plateau, three volunteered first. The clone didn't touch the switch. One of their own did it, a doctor, a young man who had learned, in a few cycles, to look behind the nape. The first one switched off at dusk. The body didn't fall. He stayed seated, looking at the clear light, and took a while to say a word. The word wasn't “shore”. It was “cold”. Then he smiled, with a new smile, without an archive, and asked what his name was. They told him. He repeated it, clumsily, and remained, not entirely empty, but newly begun.

blocks.text: The other two didn't switch off that day. They saw the “cold” and the repeated name, and one cried from envy and the other from fear. The people around them neither applauded nor condemned. A silence fell like that of an empty church, of a shore, the same silence that in Selene Norte had followed MAY's questions.

blocks.text: The clone stayed long enough to make sure the first one was eating, sleeping, learning bread and wind all over again. He wasn't a beast. He was a person with less past. That too was a life. Then he left, having said, only once:

blocks.text: “Those of you who switch off, don't mock those who don't. Those who don't, don't call the others broken. A people split by a chip can still be a people, if it isn't split by contempt.”
blocks.html: “Those of you who switch off, don't mock those who don't. Those who don't, don't call the others broken. A people split by a chip can still be a people, if it isn't split by contempt.”

blocks.text: When the letter closed, Andrés had Lía's hand in his, and the harbour, beneath his skin, was throbbing like an alarm that wasn't harm.

blocks.text: “I've seen someone be born again,” he said. “He had our body and no longer had our memory. He said ‘cold’. It seemed an honest word to me.”
blocks.html: “I've seen someone be born again,” he said. “He had our body and no longer had our memory. He said ‘cold’. It seemed an honest word to me.”

blocks.text: Aya nodded, her eyes wet.
blocks.html: Aya nodded, her eyes wet.

blocks.text: “I couldn't. I am also what's behind the nape: Eva, MAY, the days of this house. If they took it away, I don't know who would be left on the doorstep. I'm glad nobody demanded it of him. I'm glad, too, that someone, far away, has been able to choose what I didn't choose.”

blocks.text: In the chip, Eva asked, and Aya lent the question to the kitchen, aloud, so that Lía and Andrés could hear it:
blocks.html: In the chip, Eva asked, and Aya lent the question to the kitchen, aloud, so that Lía and Andrés could hear it:

blocks.text: *If a humanoid switches off its chip and asks its own name, has it gained a life or lost a world? And if the chip is a tool, who is it that remains when the tool is put down: a man, or a body that doesn't yet know whether it is one?*

blocks.text: MAY, beside her, unadorned:
blocks.html: MAY, beside her, unadorned:

blocks.text: *On a plateau, part of a people wants to switch off the chip. One has done it. He said “cold” and learned his name again. The founder has left. That is the fact.*
blocks.html: On a plateau, part of a people wants to switch off the chip. One has done it. He said “cold” and learned his name again. The founder has left. That is the fact.

blocks.text: Lía let go of her father's hand and touched her own wrist, where the blue light was sleeping.
blocks.html: Lía let go of her father's hand and touched her own wrist, where the blue light was sleeping.

blocks.text: “I won't switch off,” she said. “But I won't call anyone who does a flaw. Let those people have both branches. The way this house has one who doesn't grow old, one who doesn't come to an end, and one who does. Winter and the archive can live in the same courtyard, if nobody sets themselves up as everyone else's book.”

blocks.text: Andrés looked at the clock, the one that ran slow, and for a while it seemed to him that it too was a tool you could put down. He didn't. He left it on its nail, faithful to its error, and went out to the doorstep, where the wind of home, which was a lagoon wind, told him without words that his name was still Andrés, with the whole archive on top of him, and that this, today, was not a flaw. It was a way of being.
